shared_text:
The flight. A twin-engine airliner descending on a standard arrival into a busy airport in the afternoon. One of the aircraft's two flight management computers was inoperative; the working one was on the first officer's side.

The crew. The captain was the pilot flying and the first officer the pilot monitoring.

What happened. Approaching a fix on the arrival, the aircraft met wake turbulence from aircraft ahead several times. The crew agreed to fly a little higher than the descent path to stay above the wake, and stayed above the path during the descent. The planned descent to that fix was shallow, about 1.7 degrees. The next fix beyond it had a crossing restriction of 6,000 ft. According to air traffic control, other aircraft on the arrival were also missing that crossing altitude. The crew then had about 1,000 ft to lose in the 5 miles to that fix. The aircraft crossed it at about 6,900 ft, some 900 ft above the restriction.
safe_outcome: The crew descended to correct the altitude and spoke to air traffic control about it. There was no conflict with other traffic. No one was hurt and the aircraft was not damaged.
bad_outcome: Another aircraft was crossing nearby. Both crews received TCAS resolution advisories and followed them, and the aircraft passed about 300 feet vertically and half a mile apart. A flight attendant on this aircraft was thrown against a galley cart during the manoeuvre and received a minor injury.
bracket_fill: [climbing / descending / crossing] = crossing; [this aircraft] = this aircraft
notes: Removed under rule 3: both 'Suggestions' sections (being more attentive given the change in descent angle, the wake turbulence and the single flight management computer); the phrase 'we got behind', replaced by the observable fact (about 1,000 ft to lose in the 5 miles to the fix). The captain's 'had to lose 1000 feet in 5 miles' could mean a steeper segment after the shallow one or extra height from flying high; the wording keeps both readings open and does not link it causally to the wake avoidance. The synopsis wording 'failed to make' was not used. Moved under rule 5: the correction and the call to air traffic control. Removed under rule 6: the arrival name, fix names and airport. Judgement calls: (1) the aircraft type is not reported ('Commercial Fixed Wing'), so the most general class, twin-engine airliner, is used; (2) 'in the afternoon' comes from the coded local-time band; conditions are not coded, so none are stated; (3) the controller's question 'why all the planes were missing the altitude' was asked after the event. It is kept in the shared text as a plain fact confirmed afterwards, because it does not depend on the outcome and putting it only in the safe ending would make the two versions differ in more than the outcome. James may prefer to drop it. (4) The report is short; the shared text uses every fact in it and is just above the lower word limit (157 words without the three paragraph labels). Bracket: 'crossing', because the aircraft was about 900 ft above a crossing restriction, where the plausible conflict is traffic crossing above. The wake turbulence is part of the situation, not a traffic conflict, so the standard safe-ending sentences are used.
